newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin ill at tough time in foreign relations.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin ill at tough time in foreign relations.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's pneumonia has laid him low at a delicate time for Russian diplomacy, when his personal involvement will be vital to help steer Moscow and the West through a difficult period.

Yeltsin has a hectic schedule of meetings with foreign leaders in the next few weeks which will go a long way to determining how Russia reacts when NATO issues invitations to some former Soviet allies to join, probably next July.

Doctors say the 65-year-old president will need about three weeks to recover, which would allow him to take part in all or most of those meetings. Russian leaders would continue to deliver his message even if he were absent himself.

But if Yeltsin's health forces him to take a back seat in foreign policy, breakthroughs on issues such as NATO enlargment will be much harder and the danger of a deterioration in relations with the West this year would increase.

"The odds are that there would be a drift in policy without Yeltsin. No one but Yeltsin can make radical decisions on issues such as NATO," said Andrei Kortunov, a political analyst who heads the Russian Science Foundation.

"There could probably be drifts in economic policy and political reforms as well, but foreign policy is much more vulnerable to Yeltsin's absence because he has made it very much his presidential foreign policy."
As president, Yeltsin is ultimately responsible for policy and all major decisions. If his health permits, he can dictate policy from wherever he recuperates after leaving hospital.
But recent experience is not encouraging.

Foreign policy drifted during his almost six-month absence from the Kremlin last year when important decisions were put on hold. This was partly because of his heart problems and partly because of presidential election campaigns in Russia and the United States which were dominated by domestic issues.
"One thing is clear -- without the president, nothing moves in Russia," a European diplomat said.
A policy drift now, when tough decisions lie ahead on NATO expansion, would involve more risks than last year.

"If there is no Yeltsin around, the West may feel there is no one to give their message to and no one to act on the message. This could affect negotiations and mean Russia's position is ignored when expansion goes ahead," Kortunov said.

That would be disastrous for Yeltsin. A failure to convince Russian voters that Moscow has won as many concessions as possible from NATO over expansion would strengthen the hand of his politicial opponents.
It could also tempt Moscow to carry out its threats to apply unspecified "adequate measures" -- a response which could bring on a chill in international relations.
"There is a danger of a very serious cooling in relations between Russia and the United States," said Sergei Rogov, head of Moscow's USA and Canada Institute thinktank.
Such fears, and Russia's desire to win concessions from NATO over expansion, mean diplomatic efforts to reach a breakthrough on NATO expansion and appease Moscow will be intense.
They are also behind Russian officials' busy diplomatic schedule in the next few weeks, starting with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana's scheduled visit on January 19.
Yeltsin is due to meet French President Jacques Chirac in Moscow on February 2 and to visit The Hague to meet the European Union's president, Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, on February 4.

The president is also expected to meet British Prime Minister John Major in the near future and to hold a summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton in March. He had talks with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl last week.

Although Russia appears to have toughened its resistance to NATO expansion this year, Western leaders hope that the countries' mutual interest in keeping relations on track will -- with or without Yeltsin at the helm -- prevent a new chill.

"The decision about opening NATO has already been taken, but we are doing our best to construct solid and long-lasting relations with Russia," Solana said during a visit to Washington on Thursday. "NATO needs that relationship and Russia needs that relationship."
